strengths: Addresses an important question: whether optimization methods that improve generalization can simultaneously increase membership leakage.
The influence-based stratification provides an interesting exploratory view of SAM's gains on atypical examples, supported by comparisons with SGD and SWA.
Experiments cover four image and tabular datasets, several attack types, and additional image-model architectures. The appendix provides training hyperparameters and results for individual attacks.

SharpReg is simple to incorporate into training and produces substantial reported attack reductions. On CIFAR-100, single-query attack accuracy decreases from 76.68% to 59.64%, while test accuracy decreases from 79.92% to 75.86%.
weaknesses: The central memorization explanation is not established. Section 3 uses precomputed influence scores from SGD-trained models on CIFAR-100; it does not measure how SAM changes memorization. Better accuracy on examples that require memorization under SGD could also reflect better representations under SAM. Direct influence measurements, subgroup-removal experiments, and controls for baseline example difficulty are needed to support the proposed mechanism.

The new entropy metric has an unresolved definition problem. Appendix C.1 assigns 2,153 test examples with entirely zero influence vectors to the highest-entropy bucket, although Equation (3) has an undefined normalization in this case. Normalizing absolute influences also discards their magnitude and sign. The interpretation of this metric as a memorization spectrum needs validation and sensitivity analyses for zero handling, estimation noise, and bucket boundaries.

There are substantial inconsistencies in the attack reporting. Under balanced membership evaluation, the correctness attack in Equation (8) has accuracy (training accuracy + 1 - test accuracy)/2. Table 4 therefore implies approximately 59.84% for CIFAR-100 SGD and 59.19% for SAM, whereas Table 3 reports 77.04% and 79.10%. Exact membership balancing and evaluated subsets are insufficiently specified. These discrepancies require reconciliation before the privacy results can be considered reliable.

The privacy claims are broader than the evidence. Table 1 shows that SAM reduces multi-query attack accuracy on CIFAR-100 from 69.18% to 65.41% and on CIFAR-10 from 56.36% to 54.01%; this pattern also appears across architectures. Purchase-100 shows a small single-query increase relative to the reported variability and no generalization improvement. The conclusions should distinguish attack settings and investigate sensitivity beyond the fixed SAM radius.

SharpReg's claimed separate overfitting-control mechanism is not justified. For xi < 1, Equation (5) equals (1 - xi) times Equation (4) with effective sharpness coefficient lambda/(1 - xi). Although the appendix acknowledges a parameter simplification, varying xi changes loss scaling and effective sharpness weighting rather than introducing an independent regularizer. Comparisons that account for learning-rate scaling are needed to substantiate its additional contribution.

The defense evaluation does not establish a competitive privacy–utility tradeoff against simple regularization or early-stopped SGD at comparable accuracy. Moreover, Table 4 shows SELENA achieving both higher test accuracy and lower attack accuracy than the selected SharpReg configuration on CIFAR-100 and Texas-100. Runtime and memory measurements are missing to quantify the proposed method's potential efficiency advantage.

Privacy evaluation and reproducibility remain incomplete: there are no stronger likelihood-ratio attacks or true-positive rates at low false-positive rates, and the five reported repetitions vary attack-data splits without clearly establishing independent victim-training variability. Links to upstream implementations do not fully specify the proposed implementation and evaluation protocol.
